passage: On Republic Day morning the village school gave out bibs from a sack without looking: red or blue. Nandini got red. Her best friend Rehana got blue. By the first race Nandini was jumping up and down. 'Red is the best! Red is fastest!' Rehana stuck out her tongue. 'Blue is best. Red is for tomatoes.' They had shared a slate that very morning. Now they sat on opposite sides of the line, cheering and booing. When a red boy tripped, Rehana clapped. At lunch, bibs off, they shared their parathas again as if nothing had happened.

qa.q: How were the bibs given out?
qa.a: From a sack without looking.

qa.q: How did Nandini feel after getting a red bib?
qa.a: Nandini felt excited and proud, jumping and shouting that red was the best.

qa.q: What could the teacher do to keep the fun but soften the booing?
qa.a: Cheer good running from both colours and mix the teams in the next game, so the children see the colours don't make anyone better.

qa.q: What would change if Nandini and Rehana had both got red?
qa.a: They would probably have cheered together instead of booing each other, since the colour alone split them.

grounding: On a village sports day two young friends given random bibs instantly cheer their own colour and boo the other.

passage: On the snow day at the Oslo kindergarten, the teacher pulled coloured hats from a basket without looking: yellow or green. Lars got yellow. Hana got green. Within five minutes Lars was shouting, 'Yellow team is the strongest!' and building a snow wall with the other yellows. Hana and the greens built their own wall across the yard. 'Greens are babies!' called a yellow boy. Hana marched over, cheeks red. 'Greens are better! We have Hana!' When the teacher asked Lars why yellow was better, he thought hard. 'Because I'm yellow,' he said, as if that settled it.

qa.q: What did the teacher pull from the basket?
qa.a: Coloured hats, yellow or green.

qa.q: How did Hana feel when a yellow boy called the greens babies?
qa.a: Hana felt angry and protective of her team, cheeks red, marching over to defend it.

qa.q: What could the teacher do next?
qa.a: Mix the colours for a new game or give both walls a shared goal, like building one big castle together.

qa.q: How might the teacher see the children's quick loyalty?
qa.a: The teacher might find it funny but notice how fast random hats made each child feel their side was best.

grounding: On a snow day abroad young children given random hat colours quickly decide their own team is best.

passage: The week before Diwali, Miss Joshi handed out orange and purple bibs for the relay, straight out of the box. Reena got orange, Zeenat purple. At snacks Reena spread her mat and said, 'Only oranges sit here.' Zeenat, who sat with her every single day, stood holding her tiffin. 'But I'm your friend.' 'You're purple,' Reena said, as if it were a rule. Miss Joshi knelt down. 'Who decided who got which colour?' Reena thought. 'You did. From the box.' 'So is purple worse?' Reena looked at Zeenat's bib, then moved over. 'Purples can sit too.'

qa.q: What colours were the bibs?
qa.a: Orange and purple.

qa.q: What was Reena feeling when she said 'Only oranges sit here'?
qa.a: Reena felt proud of her orange team and sure it came first, as if belonging made a rule.

qa.q: What did Miss Joshi's questions help Reena notice?
qa.a: That the colours came at random from a box, so purple wasn't worse and the new rule made no sense.

qa.q: What is it like for Zeenat to be told 'You're purple'?
qa.a: Zeenat feels hurt and confused, shut out by a friend over a colour she didn't choose.

grounding: In a preschool before Diwali a girl given a random bib colour quickly makes it an 'us and them' rule.

subtype: Pride in the group and dislike of rivals [Actor]
passage: December sports day at the Chandigarh school, and Baljeet had painted his cheeks green for Green House. He had shouted himself hoarse all morning. In the last relay Yellow House overtook Green by a hand. Baljeet felt it like a punch in his own stomach. When Kavitha from Yellow skipped past waving a ribbon, he heard himself yell, 'Cheaters! Yellow is for cowards!' A few Greens laughed. Kavitha stopped. 'We didn't cheat. We just ran faster.' She walked away, her ribbon hanging. Baljeet's green paint had started to run. He wasn't sure any more why he had said it.

qa.q: What had Baljeet painted on his cheeks?
qa.a: Green, for Green House.

qa.q: How did Baljeet feel when Yellow overtook Green?
qa.a: Baljeet felt hurt, as if the loss were a punch in his own stomach.

qa.q: What could Baljeet do after sports day?
qa.a: He could apologise to Kavitha and congratulate Yellow, keeping his pride in Green without mocking the others.

qa.q: How did Kavitha feel when called a cheater?
qa.a: Kavitha felt hurt and wronged, her celebration spoiled, since Yellow had simply run faster.

grounding: At a winter sports day a boy's pride in his house turns to hurt and mockery when the rival house wins.

subtype: Pride in the group and dislike of rivals [Actor]
passage:
'Out! OUT!' Gautam leapt up on the terrace wall. 'Sector 12 is finished!'
'Sit down,' said his sister Kalyani. 'Diwali sweets everywhere.'
'Sector 9 forever! Sector 12 kids are crybabies!'
Then Sector 12's batter hit a six into the park. Then another. Gautam's face fell.
'It's just a colony match,' Kalyani said.
'It's MY team!' He thumped the wall. 'All Sector 12 people are show-offs.'
'Masi lives in Sector 12.'
'...Not her.'
'And Arun. Your best friend.'
Gautam went quiet, arms folded. 'I don't hate Arun.'
'Then maybe don't hate a whole sector because of two sixes.'
He sighed and sat down beside her, still watching.

qa.q: What did Sector 12's batter hit?
qa.a: A six into the park, and then another.

qa.q: How did Gautam feel when the sixes came?
qa.a: Gautam felt hurt and angry, as if the loss were personal because it was his team.

qa.q: How could Gautam enjoy supporting Sector 9 without mocking others?
qa.a: He could cheer his team loudly but clap good shots from either side, remembering people like Masi and Arun.

qa.q: How does Kalyani see Gautam's outburst?
qa.a: Kalyani finds it over the top and gently reminds him that people he loves are on the other side.

grounding: During Diwali holidays a boy's warm team pride slides into mocking the rival colony until his sister steps in.

subtype: Pride in the group and dislike of rivals [Actor]
passage: Last Onam, our school held the inter-house quiz, and I was captain of Blue House. I'm Jeevan, and I wore my blue badge even to bed. Salma was captain of Red. In the final round Red won by one question, about the capital of Peru. I felt it in my chest, as if someone had taken something of mine. So in the corridor I said loudly, 'Red only won because Salma's father is a teacher.' It wasn't true. Everyone knew it wasn't true. Salma's face went still. Now I think I wanted Blue to be better so badly that I had to make Red worse. I apologised a week later, at the pookalam competition. She accepted, but she didn't smile. I still wear the badge. I just don't say those things.

qa.q: What was the final quiz question about?
qa.a: The capital of Peru.

qa.q: How did Jeevan feel when Red won by one question?
qa.a: Jeevan felt hurt, as if something personal had been taken, and resentful towards Red.

qa.q: What could Jeevan do at the next house event?
qa.a: Jeevan could cheer Blue proudly and congratulate Red if they win, keeping the pride without mocking the other side.

qa.q: How did Salma feel hearing the comment about her father?
qa.a: Salma felt hurt and insulted, her face going still at an unfair accusation.

grounding: A child looks back on house pride at an Onam quiz turning into a false jibe at the rival captain.

passage:
Friday: Vandana's favourite band, seven boys from Seoul she had followed for four years, won a big music award. She screamed, hugged her pillow, posted twelve times and felt, all evening, as if she had won something too.
Monday: her brother Divyansh read out a comment at breakfast: 'Their music is fake, made in a factory.' Vandana's face burned. She argued for twenty minutes, then slammed her door and cried, as if he had insulted her, not them.
Thursday: at school, her friend Rukhsar said she liked Vandana's drawings more than any band. Vandana was surprised how warm that felt. That night, when Divyansh teased again, she shrugged. 'They're great. I'm also great. You can dislike them.' Divyansh blinked. 'Who are you?'

qa.q: How long had Vandana followed the band?
qa.a: Four years.

qa.q: Why did Vandana cry after the breakfast argument?
qa.a: Vandana felt hurt and insulted, as if the comment about the band were an attack on her own self.

qa.q: What helped Vandana feel steadier by Thursday?
qa.a: Being valued for her own drawings reminded her that her worth didn't rest only on the band.

qa.q: How might Divyansh feel when Vandana shrugs off his teasing?
qa.a: Divyansh is surprised, even a little thrown, since his sister no longer reacts as if personally attacked.

grounding: Over a week a teenage girl's mood rises and falls with her favourite band's fortunes, until her own worth steadies her.

passage: Baljeet, you've been sulking since your school lost the zonal final, so let me tell you about me at fifteen. I went to a small girls' school in Jalandhar, and our hockey team was everything to me. When we won, I walked taller for weeks. When a girl from the convent school laughed that village schools can't hold a stick, I pushed her into a puddle and got suspended for three days. Rashmi Bua, the troublemaker. I felt their insult on my own skin. My father didn't shout. He asked me, 'If the team lost tomorrow, would you be less?' I couldn't answer. That year I started writing for the school magazine, something that was just mine. When the team lost the next final, I was sad. But I was still me.

qa.q: How long was Rashmi suspended?
qa.a: For three days.

qa.q: How did Rashmi feel when the convent girl mocked the team?
qa.a: Rashmi felt insulted and furious, as if the mockery were aimed at her own skin.

qa.q: Rashmi's father asked if she would be less if the team lost. Why was that a turning point?
qa.a: It made Rashmi see her worth was resting on the team, which led her to build something of her own in magazine writing.

qa.q: How might the convent girl have felt after being pushed?
qa.a: She was probably shocked and upset, never expecting a joke to end in a puddle.

grounding: An aunt recalls a teenage self-worth tied to her school hockey team, and how she found something of her own.

passage: The rain delayed the inter-state under-16 football final by two hours, and Maria spent them refreshing comments on her phone. Goa's team, her team, her state, was playing Kerala. When Kerala scored in the eighty-ninth minute and won, someone on the stream wrote, 'Goans only know how to party.' Maria felt it like a slap. She typed an angry reply, then another, then a third about Kerala. Her friend Sudha, beside her in the wet stand, put a hand over the screen. 'Maria. You didn't lose. They did. And that comment is one idiot.' Maria stared at her half-typed reply, full of words she'd hate anyone to say about Goa. Her hands were shaking. She deleted it slowly and pulled up her hood. 'It still feels like they insulted me.' 'I know,' Sudha said. 'That's why I stopped you.'

qa.q: What did someone write on the stream?
qa.a: 'Goans only know how to party.'

qa.q: How did Maria feel when she read the comment?
qa.a: Maria felt insulted and angry, as if the slap were aimed at her personally.

qa.q: What helped Maria not post the angry reply?
qa.a: Sudha's steady hand and words separated Maria's worth from the team's loss and one stranger's comment.

qa.q: Why did Sudha stop Maria?
qa.a: Sudha could see Maria was taking the insult personally and about to write the same kind of thing she hated, so she stepped in.

grounding: On a rainy final day a teenage girl feels an insult to her state's team as an insult to herself, and a friend steadies her.

passage: The Howrah train was delayed six hours, so Arnab spent the night at Bengaluru station with whoever else was stuck. At 11 pm, sharing a bench with a family from Kolkata, he was all Bengali, arguing about fish curry and the best sweet shop in Bhowanipore. At 1 am, when a group of engineering students from another college sat nearby, he was suddenly an engineer, debating circuits and complaining about exams. At 3 am the station TV showed a cricket replay, and he was just a fan, yelling with strangers from Kerala and Punjab. His classmate Binita, travelling with him, laughed. 'You've been three different people tonight.' Arnab thought about it. 'Maybe that's good. If I was only Bengali, I'd have spent the night alone.'

qa.q: How long was the train delayed?
qa.a: Six hours.

qa.q: How did Arnab feel when Binita said he had been three people?
qa.a: Arnab felt amused and thoughtful, seeing his shifting identities as something good.

qa.q: Why is noticing many identities useful for Arnab?
qa.a: It keeps any one label from taking over and lets him connect with very different people.

qa.q: How does Binita see Arnab's night?
qa.a: Binita finds it funny and notices how he changed with each group.

grounding: On a long station night a young man finds different identities coming forward with different company.

passage: In her Delhi law college, Farida felt like five people in one Tuesday. At the 9 am moot court she was a future lawyer, sharp and fast. At lunch with the Lucknow students she was a Lucknowi, teasing Delhi people about their manners. On the football ground she was a goalkeeper, nothing else. Then at the evening seminar on religion and law, every head turned to her when the professor asked for 'a Muslim perspective', and she felt the other four people vanish. Her classmate Siddharth caught her face afterwards. 'You looked annoyed.' 'I am. I'm a lot of things. In there I was only one.' He thought. 'I get it. At home I'm only the eldest son.' They walked to the metro together, a lawyer, a Lucknowi, a goalkeeper and her friend.

qa.q: What was Farida on the football ground?
qa.a: A goalkeeper, nothing else.

qa.q: How did Farida feel when every head turned to her in the seminar?
qa.a: Farida felt annoyed and resentful, reduced to a single label while the rest of her vanished.

qa.q: What could the professor have done differently?
qa.a: Invite views from anyone interested instead of turning to Farida as the representative, letting students speak as individuals.

qa.q: How does Siddharth relate to Farida's frustration?
qa.a: Siddharth understands, since at home he is reduced to being the eldest son.

grounding: A law student feels different identities come forward in different rooms and resents being reduced to just one.

passage:
'Why do you talk differently on the phone with your mother?' Anirban asked, as Pooja hung up.
'Differently how?'
'You went full Bhojpuri. Here you're all "bro, the code's broken".'
Pooja laughed. 'At home I'm the city girl who's gone modern. In the hostel I'm "the Bihari", which I hate. In the coding club I'm just the one who fixes bugs.'
'Which one's real?'
'All of them. Depends who's in the room.'
'Doesn't that feel fake?'
'No. If I were only "the Bihari", people could put me in one box. This way no box fits.'
Anirban grinned. 'So in the canteen, which one is buying me samosas?'
'The one who fixes bugs. The Bihari is broke.'

qa.q: What language did Pooja use with her mother?
qa.a: Full Bhojpuri.

qa.q: How does Pooja feel about being called 'the Bihari' in the hostel?
qa.a: Pooja resents and hates it, because it squeezes Pooja into one box.

qa.q: Why is being many things at once helpful for Pooja?
qa.a: It keeps any one label from taking over, so no single box can define Pooja.

qa.q: How does Anirban react to Pooja's switching?
qa.a: Anirban is curious at first, wondering if it feels fake, then accepts it and jokes about samosas.

grounding: A student explains feeling Bihari, coder or city girl depending on who is present, which keeps one label from taking over.

passage: You asked about the football club. Okay. I'm Tenzin, I'm twenty-four, and when I started coaching the kids' team in our Delhi colony, I only wanted Tibetan boys. It felt natural. My people, my language, my pride. Then Sachin, a Punjabi boy from the next lane, came every evening and stood by the fence. Good feet. I kept saying 'next season'. One day I caught myself thinking, he's not one of us. And I felt ashamed, because that's exactly what people have said about us. So I changed the idea of 'us'. We became the colony team: anyone from these lanes. Sachin plays left wing now. The Tibetan boys still sing our songs before matches, and now Sachin knows them too. I'm still proud of where I come from. I just don't need anyone to be less for that.

qa.q: Where does Sachin play now?
qa.a: Left wing.

qa.q: How did Tenzin feel on catching the thought 'he's not one of us'?
qa.a: Tenzin felt ashamed, knowing people had said the same about Tibetans.

qa.q: What did Tenzin do to widen the shared identity?
qa.a: He made the club the colony team, open to anyone from the lanes, keeping Tibetan pride without excluding others.

qa.q: How might Sachin have felt standing by the fence every evening?
qa.a: Sachin probably felt hopeful but left out, waiting for a chance that kept being put off.

grounding: A young coach notices the pull to favour his own community and widens 'us' to the whole colony while keeping his pride.

passage: I'm Hansa, and I've sat in the same open office as Tejas since our two companies merged last year. For months it was 'us' and 'them': the old Pune team and the Mumbai lot, different lunch tables, jokes in the group chat. Tejas was one of the loudest Pune voices at first. Then something shifted. At a planning meeting I watched him catch himself mid-joke about 'Mumbai slowness', stop and say, 'Actually, we're one team now, and your data saved us last quarter.' The next week he started a Friday cricket match: mixed sides, drawn from a hat. When someone from Pune mocked a Mumbai colleague's accent, Tejas said, 'Not here.' I don't know what changed in his head. But the lunch tables have been pushed together since March.

qa.q: How are the Friday cricket sides chosen?
qa.a: Mixed sides, drawn from a hat.

qa.q: What might Tejas have been feeling when he stopped mid-joke?
qa.a: Tejas perhaps felt a flash of discomfort or shame, noticing the pull to mock the other group.

qa.q: Which of Tejas's actions best widened the shared identity?
qa.a: Calling everyone one team, crediting the Mumbai data, mixing the cricket sides and stopping mockery with 'Not here'.

qa.q: How has Hansa's view of the office changed?
qa.a: Hansa has watched 'us and them' fade, noticing the lunch tables pushed together since March.

grounding: A colleague watches a young man loosen an office us-them split by building a shared team identity and stopping mockery.

passage:
September: at his daughter's school in Pune, Tushar joined the parents' chats and found two: one for Marathi-speaking parents, one for everyone else. He joined the Marathi one, felt at home, and laughed along at jokes about 'outsider' parents who never volunteered.
October: at sports day, the 'outsider' dad, Shankar, was the one fixing the broken microphone, running the water station and carrying Tushar's own daughter to first aid when she scraped her knee. Tushar stood with his coffee, uneasy.
December: Tushar proposed merging the chats into one, 'Class 1B parents'. A few grumbled. He posted in Marathi, Hindi and English, thanked Shankar publicly for sports day, and set a rule: no jokes about anyone's home state. By the Christmas party, Shankar and Tushar were co-organising the snacks, arguing happily about vada pav versus samosas.

qa.q: What did Shankar do at sports day?
qa.a: Fixed the broken microphone, ran the water station and carried Tushar's daughter to first aid.

qa.q: What was Tushar feeling as he stood with his coffee at sports day?
qa.a: Tushar felt uneasy and a little ashamed, seeing the 'outsider' he had laughed at helping his own daughter.

qa.q: Which step best widened the us-them line?
qa.a: Merging the chats into one 'Class 1B parents' group with a no-jokes rule, which built a shared identity as parents.

qa.q: How might Shankar feel being thanked publicly?
qa.a: Shankar would likely feel recognised and welcomed, no longer treated as an outsider.

grounding: Over a term a young father notices his in-group favouritism and builds a wider identity of fellow parents.

subtype: Feeling poor next to a friend [Actor]
passage: The day after Christmas in Lisbon, Bilal rode into the square on a shiny red bicycle with gears, a new phone buzzing in his pocket. Rafael had got a football, a book and new trainers, and at breakfast he had been thrilled. Now, watching Bilal show off the gears, something sank in his chest. His trainers suddenly looked ordinary. At home he pushed his dinner around. 'Aren't you happy with your presents?' his mother asked. 'I was,' Rafael said, 'until I saw Bilal's.' His mother sat beside him. 'Were the trainers different at breakfast?' He thought. They weren't. Only Bilal's bike had changed how they looked.

qa.q: What did Rafael get for Christmas?
qa.a: A football, a book and new trainers.

qa.q: What did Rafael feel watching Bilal show off the gears?
qa.a: Rafael felt a sinking sadness, his own presents suddenly seeming ordinary.

qa.q: How did Rafael's mother's question help?
qa.a: It helped him notice that nothing about his own gifts had changed; only the comparison made them feel worse.

qa.q: How might Bilal feel if he knew Rafael was sad?
qa.a: Bilal might be surprised or a bit sorry, since he was only excited about his bike, not trying to hurt anyone.

grounding: After Christmas abroad a boy who has enough feels sad next to a friend's new bicycle and phone.

subtype: Feeling poor next to a friend [Actor]
passage: On the first day back after Diwali, Class 5 buzzed with new things. Usha had a smartwatch that lit up, and everyone crowded round her desk. Vishal had new shoes and a whole box of kaju katli from his Nani, and that morning he'd felt rich. Now, sitting at the back, he tucked his feet under the bench. His shoes looked plain. His tiffin felt babyish. When the teacher asked the class to write about their Diwali, he wrote only two lines. At break Usha came over. 'Can I have some kaju katli? My Nani never makes it.' Vishal blinked, opened the box and watched her eyes widen. Something in his chest loosened.

qa.q: What did Usha have that lit up?
qa.a: A smartwatch.

qa.q: Why did Vishal tuck his feet under the bench?
qa.a: Vishal felt sad and a little ashamed, his new shoes suddenly seeming plain next to Usha's watch.

qa.q: What could the teacher do to help children like Vishal after festivals?
qa.a: Invite children to share favourite moments rather than new things, so comparing possessions matters less.

qa.q: How does Usha see Vishal's kaju katli?
qa.a: Usha finds it special, wishing her own Nani made it, which shows Vishal has things others envy too.

grounding: At school after Diwali a boy who felt rich that morning feels poor beside a classmate's new watch.

subtype: Feeling poor next to a friend [Actor]
passage:
Monday, first day of the Ganesh holidays: Rukmini rode her old blue cycle round the Hubli colony, bell ringing, happy as anything.
Wednesday: Deepak from the second floor came down with a brand-new cycle with gears and a basket, and a phone clipped to the handle for music. Rukmini's blue cycle suddenly looked rusty. That evening she refused to ride it and told Amma, 'We're poor.' Amma laughed, then saw her face. 'Are we? You have a cycle, books, a festival. What changed since Monday?' Rukmini had no answer.
The next Sunday: at the immersion procession, Deepak's chain came off and he had to walk. Rukmini gave him a lift on her carrier, both of them laughing. Her old cycle had never felt better.

qa.q: What colour was Rukmini's old cycle?
qa.a: Blue.

qa.q: What was Rukmini feeling when she told Amma 'We're poor'?
qa.a: Rukmini felt sad and hurt by comparison, her happy old cycle suddenly looking rusty next to Deepak's.

qa.q: How did Amma's question help Rukmini?
qa.a: It showed that nothing about her own life had changed since Monday; only the comparison made her feel poor.

qa.q: How might Deepak have felt getting a lift on the old cycle?
qa.a: Deepak was probably relieved and grateful, laughing along, not caring that the cycle was old.

grounding: Across a festival week a girl who has enough feels poor next to a neighbour's new cycle, and the feeling passes.

passage: At the tuition centre in Ahmedabad, the mock-test marks went up on the whiteboard. Zubin had 88, his best ever. For three seconds he was thrilled. Then he saw Sangeeta's name above his, 92, and Harsh's, 91. His chest went tight. He didn't look at the twenty names below him. On the bus home he kept replaying it: same classes, so why were they always just ahead? It felt unfair, like being cheated in a race. His phone buzzed: his father, 'How did it go?' Zubin typed 'bad', then stopped. Eighty-eight. Last term it had been 71. He deleted 'bad' and wrote, 'Better than last time.' It didn't feel better yet. But it was true.

qa.q: What was Zubin's mark last term?
qa.a: Last term it had been 71.

qa.q: What did Zubin feel when he saw Sangeeta's 92?
qa.a: Zubin felt a tight, unfair sense of being cheated, his joy at 88 vanishing.

qa.q: What helped Zubin see his result more fairly?
qa.a: Comparing with his own past, 71 last term, instead of only with the two people just ahead.

qa.q: How might the twenty students below Zubin see his 88?
qa.a: They might see it as an excellent score and envy him, just as he envied those above.

grounding: At a tuition centre a teenager feels cheated by peers just ahead despite his own best-ever mark.

passage:
Dear Trisha Didi,
You asked why I sounded grumpy on the call. Okay, honestly: it's the girls in my class. Not the super-rich ones; I don't even think about them. It's Ritika and Maya, who are just a bit ahead. Maya went to Singapore in the holidays; we went to Nani's village. Ritika has a new phone; mine is Papa's old one. I got 84 in science and felt amazing for exactly one minute, until Ritika said she got 87. I know we have enough. We have a nice flat, Mummy makes the best rajma, and Papa never says no to books. But I still feel cheated, as if life gave them the bigger piece. Is that awful? How did you stop feeling like this in college?
Love,
Aadhya

qa.q: Where did Maya go in the holidays?
qa.a: To Singapore.

qa.q: How does Aadhya feel about Ritika and Maya?
qa.a: Aadhya feels cheated and envious, as if life gave them the bigger piece, even while knowing the family has enough.

qa.q: What could Trisha Didi suggest in reply?
qa.a: She could suggest noticing whom Aadhya compares with, and sometimes looking back at Aadhya's own progress or the good things at home.

qa.q: How might Trisha Didi feel reading the letter?
qa.a: Trisha may feel tender and understanding, remembering similar feelings from her own school days.

grounding: A teenager's letter shows feeling cheated next to classmates just a step ahead, despite a decent life at home.

passage: So you want to talk about envy? Okay, I'm Indu, sixteen, and I'll go first. My cousin Manjula's family moved into a three-bedroom flat last year. We're in a two-bedroom, perfectly fine; I share a room with my sister, whatever. But every time we visit Manjula, I come home in a bad mood. Her room has a window seat. Her dad drives her to school. I start thinking our life is unfair, that we're somehow behind. Then last month our school visited a hostel for students from villages, and one of them told me she had never had a room of her own, not even a corner. On the bus back I felt so small. I'm not saying I stopped comparing. But now I notice whom I compare with. It's always the person one step ahead.

qa.q: What does Manjula's room have?
qa.a: A window seat.

qa.q: How does Indu feel after visiting Manjula?
qa.a: Indu feels grumpy and cheated, as if their own life were unfair and behind.

qa.q: What did Indu learn about how comparison works?
qa.a: That the feeling of lacking depends on whom you look at, usually the person one step ahead.

qa.q: How might the student at the hostel see Indu's two-bedroom flat?
qa.a: She would probably see it as comfortable and lucky, since she had never had a room of her own.

grounding: A teenager describes feeling deprived next to a cousin a step ahead, and noticing that the feeling depends on whom she looks at.

passage: Vikas, I can hear the bitterness when you talk about your batch's placements. Let me tell you about 1991. I was twenty-two, with an engineering degree from Nagpur. Every senior of mine had walked into a public-sector job the month he graduated. So I expected the same; I felt I was owed it. Then the economy turned and the companies stopped hiring. My friends and I sat at the tea stall every evening, angry at the government, at the seniors, at everyone. I felt robbed. For a year I refused anything 'below' me. Then my father said, 'Harish, the world didn't promise you anything. Your seniors got lucky timing.' It stung. The next week I took a job repairing pumps at a sugar factory. I hated it for six months. Then I got good at it. That factory is where I learned everything.

qa.q: What job did Harish take?
qa.a: Repairing pumps at a sugar factory.

qa.q: How did Harish feel sitting at the tea stall that year?
qa.a: Harish felt angry and robbed, sure he was owed what his seniors had got.

qa.q: Harish took the pump-repair job after his father's words. Why was that a turning point?
qa.a: It moved him from bitterness about what he felt owed to building real skills, which became the base of his career.

qa.q: How might Harish's father have felt watching the bitter year?
qa.a: His father was probably worried and frustrated, wanting Harish to stop waiting and start building.

grounding: An elder recalls graduating into a hiring freeze, feeling owed his seniors' jobs, and moving past the bitterness.

passage: The placement results came out on a rainy Friday, and Payal's name wasn't on any list. Last year every senior in her design batch had been hired by the big firms before exams. This year two companies had cancelled, and only eleven of sixty got offers. Payal stood under the canteen shed, soaked, scrolling through the seniors' celebration photos from last year. It felt like something promised had been taken from her. When Vijay, a senior, walked past and said, 'Tough year, yaar. Don't worry, something will come,' she snapped, 'Easy for you to say. You got yours.' He stopped, hurt. Then Payal saw his face and felt the heat drain out of her. 'Sorry. I just thought it would be the same for us.' Vijay sat down. 'I know. Want me to send you the freelance leads I get?'

qa.q: How many of sixty got offers this year?
qa.a: Only eleven of sixty.

qa.q: How did Payal feel scrolling through the seniors' photos?
qa.a: Payal felt bitter and robbed, as if something promised had been taken away.

qa.q: What could Payal do next with her disappointment?
qa.a: Accept Vijay's freelance leads and keep building her portfolio, turning anger into a plan for a harder year.

qa.q: How did Vijay feel when Payal snapped?
qa.a: Vijay felt hurt by her words but understood, and still offered to help.

grounding: On a rainy results day a graduate who expected a job like her seniors' feels robbed and lashes out, then steadies.

passage: In the Hyderabad flat, Tanvir scrolled through his batch's messages: 'Joined!' 'Offer letter!' Most were from the computer science section. He was in mechanical, and his branch had got a third of the offers they had been promised at admission four years ago. 'They promised,' he muttered. 'Eighty per cent placement, they said.' His sister Chandrika, eating chips on the sofa, looked up. 'Who promised?' 'The college. Everyone. And now CS gets everything and we get nothing.' He slammed the laptop shut. 'It's not fair.' Chandrika waited a minute. 'It's not fair that the brochure lied. But being angry at CS won't get you a job. What will?' Tanvir glared, then opened the laptop again and started a list of mechanical firms in the city.

qa.q: What placement rate had the college promised?
qa.a: Eighty per cent placement.

qa.q: How did Tanvir feel scrolling through the batch's messages?
qa.a: Tanvir felt angry and resentful, as if the CS section were getting what his branch was owed.

qa.q: What did Chandrika's question help Tanvir do?
qa.a: It turned his anger from the CS students towards a practical step, listing mechanical firms in the city.

qa.q: How does Chandrika see Tanvir's anger?
qa.a: Chandrika agrees the brochure was unfair but thinks anger at CS won't help him.

grounding: A graduate promised good placements feels bitter when another group gets the jobs, until his sister redirects him.

passage: Kamal had managed the dairy cooperative in Anand for a year when the grumbling started. At Diwali the milk-collection staff had got a bonus for the record monsoon season; the plant workers had not. Everyone was paid fairly by the book, but Kamal noticed the plant workers eating separately and the jokes turning sharp. Shankar, who had run the chilling plant for twenty years, stopped saying good morning. Kamal didn't wait for things to boil over. He called a meeting under the neem tree and put the bonus criteria on a chart: litres collected, new farmers signed. 'You're right that it only rewarded one kind of work,' he said. 'That's my mistake.' He proposed a new rule for next year, with a plant target too, and asked Shankar to help set it. Shankar folded his arms, then nodded slowly.

qa.q: Where did Kamal call the meeting?
qa.a: Under the neem tree.

qa.q: What did Kamal feel when Shankar stopped saying good morning?
qa.a: Kamal felt uneasy and concerned, sensing resentment building even though pay was fair.

qa.q: Why did putting the criteria on a chart help?
qa.a: It made the reasons transparent, admitted the gap honestly and invited the plant workers to shape the next rule.

qa.q: Why might Shankar have stopped saying good morning?
qa.a: Shankar likely felt left behind and unappreciated after twenty years, when only the collection staff got a bonus.

grounding: A young cooperative manager notices resentment when one group gets a bonus and eases it with open criteria and honest explanation.

passage: Fatima had been promoted to team manager at the Toronto software firm in January. By March she noticed something odd: the office-based designers had gone quiet in meetings, and Astrid, usually the first to joke, answered in single words. It took Fatima a week to find the reason. The remote engineers had been given a home-office allowance; the designers, who came in every day, got nothing extra. No one was underpaid. But to the designers it looked as if one group was valued more. Fatima went to Astrid first. 'I think the allowance feels unfair to your team. Am I right?' Astrid exhaled. 'Yes. Nobody explained it.' That afternoon Fatima wrote to the whole team, laying out why the allowance existed, and proposed a matching commuting benefit to HR.

qa.q: Who got the home-office allowance?
qa.a: The remote engineers.

qa.q: What did Fatima feel noticing Astrid's single-word answers?
qa.a: Fatima felt concerned and curious, sensing something was wrong with her usually cheerful colleague.

qa.q: What made Fatima's response effective?
qa.a: She asked directly, explained the reasons openly to everyone and proposed a fair matching benefit.

qa.q: How did Astrid feel about the allowance?
qa.a: Astrid felt left behind and a bit resentful, since nobody had explained why only the remote engineers got it.

grounding: A new manager abroad notices resentment over a perk given to one group and reduces it with openness and fair criteria.

passage: On the general ward of the Chennai hospital, the nurses' station had grown cold. Anjali, the young nurse in charge, noticed it first in small things: nobody shared snacks with the ICU team any more, and Gautam, the most cheerful nurse on nights, muttered 'VIPs' whenever an ICU nurse walked past. She asked him about it over tea at 3 am. 'The ICU got the new training trip to Bengaluru and new uniforms,' Gautam said. 'We work just as hard.' Anjali knew the pay scales were identical. But she also knew nobody had explained how the trip was chosen. The next morning she asked the nursing superintendent for the criteria, posted them on the notice board and pushed for the next training slot to go to the ward. By the end of the month the snacks were being shared again.

qa.q: What did the ICU get?
qa.a: The new training trip to Bengaluru and new uniforms.

qa.q: What did Anjali feel as she noticed the cold nurses' station?
qa.a: Anjali felt uneasy and watchful, noticing small signs of resentment between the teams.

qa.q: Why did posting the criteria help?
qa.a: It made clear how the perks were chosen, so the ward felt less left behind and could see a fair path to the next slot.

qa.q: How does Gautam feel about the ICU nurses?
qa.a: Gautam feels resentful and overlooked, seeing them as VIPs getting perks for the same hard work.

grounding: A young nurse in charge spots resentment when another team gets perks and eases it with transparent criteria.

passage:
'Tanya got team lead. Tanya! She joined four months after me.' Rekha dropped her bag on the sofa.
Her brother Sahil muted the TV. 'You're fuming.'
'I'm not fuming. I'm just... okay, I'm fuming.'
'Fair. What do you actually want?'
'The promotion!'
'Why? The title or the work?'
Rekha stopped. 'The work, I think. Leading the design side.'
'Is that in your control?'
'I could ask my manager what I'm missing. I never have.' She sat down. 'And... a year ago I was on probation, crying in the office washroom. Now I'm the one juniors ask for help.'
'So compared to last-year Rekha?'
'Way ahead.' She sighed. 'Still annoyed about Tanya.'
'Allowed. Be annoyed, and book the meeting.'

qa.q: When did Tanya join compared with Rekha?
qa.a: Four months after Rekha.

qa.q: What was Rekha feeling when she dropped her bag?
qa.a: Rekha felt envious and angry, fuming about Tanya's promotion.

qa.q: Which questions helped Rekha shift her mood?
qa.a: What she actually wants, what she can control, and how she compares with her own self of a year ago.

qa.q: How does Sahil respond to Rekha's anger?
qa.a: Sahil accepts that she's annoyed, then gently guides her from envy to a plan.

grounding: A young woman fuming at a peer's promotion asks what she wants, what she controls and how far she has come.

passage: Last spring my best friend Noor got promoted to senior analyst, and I found out from a group chat. I'm Naveen, and I'm not proud of the next hour. I sat in the car outside the office, fuming, adding up everything I'd done that she hadn't. Then I remembered a trick my old cricket coach taught me: when you're angry, ask three questions. What do I actually have? A job I'm good at, a team that trusts me, and Noor, a friend who once drove me home at 2 am when I was sick. What can I control? My next project, and asking my boss for feedback. And where was I two years ago? Unemployed, sending forty applications a month. I went back in and bought Noor a cake. I still want that promotion. I just don't want envy driving the car.

qa.q: How did Naveen find out about Noor's promotion?
qa.a: From a group chat.

qa.q: How did Naveen feel sitting in the car?
qa.a: Naveen felt envious and angry, fuming and adding up everything Noor hadn't done.

qa.q: What did the three questions help Naveen do?
qa.a: See what was already there, what could be controlled and how far things had come, so ambition stayed without envy in charge.

qa.q: How might Noor feel receiving the cake?
qa.a: Noor would likely feel touched and happy, supported by a close friend on a big day.

grounding: A young adult catches envy at a friend's promotion and widens the comparison to what they have, control and have grown from.

passage:
Career coach's note, session 4.
Madhuri, 25, arrived frustrated. Her colleague Ramesh, who started the same week, was promoted to senior accountant on Monday, and she has been 'fuming for three days'. She described checking his desk, comparing hours and replaying their appraisal meetings. I didn't argue with the feeling. Instead I asked her to list what she actually has, what she can control and where she was two years ago. Her list surprised her: a steady job she likes, a qualification finished last year while working, and a manager who asks her opinion. Two years ago she was failing her exams. Her control list was short and clear: ask her manager for a development plan, and take the audit project she had been avoiding. She left calmer. She is still ambitious, and I told her that is a good thing. Review in a month.

qa.q: When was Ramesh promoted?
qa.a: On Monday.

qa.q: How had Madhuri been feeling since Ramesh's promotion?
qa.a: Madhuri had been frustrated and envious, fuming for three days and replaying their appraisals.

qa.q: Why was asking about her own past a useful step?
qa.a: It showed how far she had come, from failing exams two years ago to a qualification and a trusting manager now, which softens envy.

qa.q: How might Ramesh feel if he knew about Madhuri's frustration?
qa.a: Ramesh might feel awkward or uneasy, since they started together and he may not know she is comparing.

grounding: A coach notes a young professional turning envy at a peer's promotion into a wider comparison and a plan, keeping her ambition.
